title: Does ‘nothing beat in person work’?
author: Bruce Daisley
summary: Bruce Daisley examines In-Person, a new book by Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington arguing that remote work degrades quality, creativity, mental health, and mentoring. He is openly skeptical, noting that the authors were funded by the Smith Richardson Foundation, whose grants aim to foster an economic climate hospitable to growth. Still, he works through the book's six claims in good faith, adding the context each leaves out. The in-person earnings forecasts were 15 percent more accurate but remote ones were 46 percent faster, and that study was not peer reviewed. Nick Bloom calls the mental health claim a gross misunderstanding of the data, since people with difficulties may retreat to home working. Daisley concludes that hybrid work captures most of the real benefits, provided in-office days are coordinated, and he closes with short items on AI slop in Amazon's reading meetings and Microsoft's document doom loop.
points: Daisley asks readers to follow the data on how much in-person time helps rather than accept the claim that hybrid working has been a disaster.
The strongest evidence for in-person work is narrow, such as one firm where co-located engineers received 22 percent more code-review comments, and it does not generalize to all teams.
The mental health claim is contested because causation may run the other way, with people struggling already choosing to work from home.
The book is accused of choosing anecdotes to fit its story, as with the Kahneman and Tversky rift, which Michael Lewis attributes to credit resentment rather than distance.
Hybrid designs that gather remote teams monthly or fund in-person lunches produced measurable gains, so coordination of office time matters more than the office itself.
quotes: Not only did I hate the book - in pursuing its hypothesis the argument is partial and at times borders on disingenuous - but I’m also a little suspicious of it.
It’s clear that some degree of in-person work is helpful for teams, but let’s honestly calculate how much.

It’s worth saying that the same research said that remote work saw a 46% increase in timeliness - remote reports were produced much quicker). This was the author’s own work and hasn’t yet been peer reviewed.
Eye-tracking suggested that staring at the screen narrows thinking.

Professor Nick Bloom has commented extensively on this research - saying that it is a ‘a gross misunderstanding of the data’, suggesting that people with mental health issues might retreat to WFH as a coping mechanism - rather than it causing their problems.
In truth Michael Lewis’s The Undoing Project, documents that their fall out was largely based on resentment over credit and recognition - not their WFH disagreements.
What is interesting is that I feel hybrid work addresses a lot of these things. Getting the best value out of in-office time requires co-ordination and collaboration.
In another study sales reps given paid-for in-person lunches with colleagues sold 15% more.
